intro: Nine old trees make one walk through the centre of Santa Cruz de Tenerife, all free, roughly four kilometres on foot. The two Indian laurel figs of Plaza del Príncipe were planted in 1864 and stand 20 metres tall. One of the four Moreton Bay figs beside the Iglesia de San Francisco measures 14.27 metres round at the base. Two dragon trees stand by a fish monument and a church bell tower, Parque García Sanabria keeps a kapok ringed by four palms, and Parque de La Granja an Australian red gum and an ombú.
meta_description: Nine old trees on one free walk through Santa Cruz de Tenerife, from laurel figs planted in 1864 to a fig 14 metres round and two dragon trees.
question_meta: The oldest dated trees in Santa Cruz de Tenerife are the laurel figs of Plaza del Príncipe, planted in 1864. Most of the city's old trees carry no age.
question_answer: The oldest dated trees in Santa Cruz de Tenerife are the two Indian laurel figs of Plaza del Príncipe, planted in 1864 according to the municipal catalogue of singular trees, which makes them about 160 years old. The Moreton Bay figs of Plaza de San Francisco were already planted by 1914, but nobody has said how long before, so they may be as old or older. Most of the city's other old trees, its dragon trees included, have no recorded age at all.
question_context: Santa Cruz has one firm date among its old trees. The municipal catalogue of singular trees, presented in 2018 by the botanists Martín Osorio and Wildpret, says the laurel figs of Plaza del Príncipe were planted in 1864, seven years after the square itself was laid out. They now stand 20 metres tall. The city's register lists them without an age, so the date rests on the catalogue as the local press reported it. The same catalogue says the four Moreton Bay figs of Plaza de San Francisco were already in the ground by 1914, and one of them has the biggest girth of any tree in the city after the cardón of El Chorrillo, 14.27 metres at the base. Their real planting date could be decades earlier. Everything else is undated. Wildpret called the tamarind of Parque García Sanabria the most veteran tree in that park, but the park opened in 1926 and nobody has dated the tree itself. The dragon trees by Plaza del Chicharro and the Iglesia de la Concepción grow no annual rings, and no one has published a count of their branching. If you know any of these ages, tell us.

faq.q: Do any of these trees charge entry?
faq.a: No. All nine stand in open squares, beside a church or in public parks, Parque García Sanabria and Parque de La Granja, and none of them charges admission.

faq.q: How long does the walk take?
faq.a: The route is roughly four kilometres, about an hour of walking before you stop at anything. The four stops in the old centre lie within a few hundred metres of each other, so that part alone takes well under an hour.

faq.q: How far apart are the stops?
faq.a: Plaza del Príncipe, Plaza del Chicharro and Plaza de San Francisco are each two or three minutes apart, and the Iglesia de la Concepción is about 400 metres further. Parque García Sanabria is roughly 650 metres north of Plaza del Príncipe, and Parque de La Granja about 1.3 to 1.5 kilometres west of that park, the longest leg of the walk.

faq.q: Which is the biggest tree in Santa Cruz?
faq.a: By girth, one of the four Moreton Bay figs in Plaza de San Francisco, 14.27 metres round at the base, though the catalogue does not say which of the four. By height, the catalogue names the laurel figs of Plaza del Príncipe, at 20 metres, and the red gum of Parque de La Granja as the tallest in the urban area.

trees.name: Indian Laurel Figs of Plaza del Príncipe

location.address: Plaza del Principe de Asturias, Santa Cruz de Tenerife

trees.story:
The square was seven years old when these figs went in. Plaza del Príncipe was laid out in 1857, and the two Indian laurel figs that now shade it were planted in 1864, according to the municipal catalogue of singular trees presented by the botanists Martín Osorio and Wildpret in 2018, as the local press reported it. The city's own register lists both trees but records no age, so that date rests on the catalogue as quoted in print. About 160 years later they stand 20 metres tall, among the tallest trees anywhere in the urban area of Santa Cruz.

The two crowns stand about 15 metres apart, and aerial roots hang from them, the habit of a fig that turns roots into extra trunks wherever they reach soil. Ficus microcarpa is planted all over the city, and the council says most of its laurels are past their hundredth year.

The catalogue's authors did not write a love letter to these two. They asked for special protection and urgent action, naming pets relieving themselves against the trunks and children playing on them. Along the Rambla, at the other end of town, the council has been replacing laurels that are dying; these are not among them.

The square is free and always open, about three minutes on foot from Plaza de la Candelaria, and it makes the obvious first stop on a walk past the old trees of the centre.

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as the tallest trees on the square, two broad fig crowns about 15 metres apart with aerial roots hanging down. They stand on the Calle del Castillo side, near the bandstand.
trees.verify_notes: Register rows FIC_MIC-1 (28.468257,-16.250429) and FIC_MIC-2 (28.468141,-16.250331) folded; two crowns about 15 m apart. Municipal catalogue (Martin Osorio and Wildpret, presented 2018) per Diario de Avisos: the laurels of Plaza del Principe were planted in 1864 and now measure 20 m, among the tallest in the urban area; the same press report says they need special protection (pets urinating, children playing) and the authors asked for urgent action. Tenerife Weekly (2022) lists the laurel of the Indies of Plaza del Principe on the singular-tree route. Two press pieces give 1864; the register carries no age. Age is the press-reported planting date, so 160 years is source-based. Plaza itself was laid out 1857 (WebTenerife) so planting 1864 is plausible, but only press says so. Species: register Ficus microcarpa; iNaturalist Ficus microcarpa observation 18 m away (2024-10-01, casual): https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/245039429. Alive: lifecheck RECENT 2025-09-27 near here. Council states Rambla laurels (different trees, Rambla end) are dying and being replaced (Tenerife Weekly 2024-10-03), not these. Small square taken in at one glance, so location_site; distinguishing: the large crowns on the Calle del Castillo side near the fountain/templete, from register coordinates only. Recognition from sources: tallest trees on the square, aerial roots.

trees.name: Moreton Bay Figs of Plaza de San Francisco

location.address: Plaza de San Francisco, Santa Cruz de Tenerife

trees.story:
One of these four figs measures 14.27 metres round at the base, and in all of Santa Cruz only the cardón of El Chorrillo, at 35.2 metres, has recorded a bigger girth. That comes from the municipal catalogue of singular trees, presented in 2018. The catalogue gives the number but not the trunk, so which of the four is the record holder is something you will have to judge standing in the square. The figure is taken at the base, where a Moreton Bay fig spreads into buttresses, so it is not a chest-height measurement either.

The four stand in a row about 20 metres apart beside the Iglesia de San Francisco. The same catalogue says they were already planted by 1914, which makes them more than a century old; how much more, nobody has published. They are four of the seven Moreton Bay figs the catalogue counts across the city.

A century in a busy square has not been gentle. The catalogue's authors asked for urgent action, starting with a fence around the trunks and the removal of the artificial lawn laid around them. They reported bicycles parked against the roots, and vandalism.

The square is free and open, about five minutes on foot from Plaza de la Candelaria and a short walk from the laurel figs of Plaza del Príncipe.

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as four big figs in a row, about 20 metres apart, with buttressed trunks and hanging aerial roots over a patch of artificial lawn. They stand beside the Iglesia de San Francisco.
trees.verify_notes: Register rows FIC_MACR-1..4 folded (28.468353/-16.248961, 28.468186/-16.249006, 28.468008/-16.249032, 28.467838/-16.249062), four figs in a row about 20 m apart. Municipal catalogue per Diario de Avisos 2018: the figs of Plaza de San Francisco were already planted in 1914; the single biggest Ficus macrophylla of the plaza has 14.27 m girth at the base (largest girth after the cardon of El Chorrillo, 35.2 m); the catalogue authors asked for urgent action: fence them and remove the artificial lawn that surrounds them, bikes were parked on them, vandalism. girth_cm 1427 is the largest of the four and a base measurement (buttressed), not chest height; which of the four is not stated. Age: planted by 1914 means at least about 110 years; upper bound is conservative guess not sourced, so treat age as over a century. Species Ficus macrophylla stated in catalogue summary and register. Alive: lifecheck RECENT 2026-05-15 (iNaturalist observations 9 to 13 m from the pins, Ficus, casual): https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/362078230 and https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/346635794. Tenerife Weekly route piece: the fig tree in Bahia Moreton in the Plaza de San Francisco. Catalogue counts seven Ficus macrophylla across Santa Cruz; the other three (FIC_MACR-5/6 in Parque Garcia Sanabria, -7 Viera y Clavijo area) are elsewhere. One collectible point: one plaza, one place to stand.

trees.name: Kapok of Parque García Sanabria

location.address: Parque Garcia Sanabria, Santa Cruz de Tenerife

trees.story:
Four palms were planted around this kapok like the columns of a temple, and at least one botanist suspected that was the idea. Wolfredo Wildpret, co-author of the city's catalogue of singular trees, walked the park with the newspaper Diario de Avisos in 2018 and passed on a theory of his colleague Pérez de Paz, who saw a masonic meaning in the arrangement. Nobody has proved it, and nobody has disproved it.

Wildpret called the ceiba another of the great wonders of Parque García Sanabria, and counted it, with the ceiba of Parque Viera y Clavijo, as one of the two trees of greatest volume in Santa Cruz. Spanish Wikipedia lists it among the largest and oldest specimens in the park. Kapok is a tropical tree, the source of the silky fibre once used to stuff life jackets and mattresses.

What nobody has published is a number. There is no recorded girth, no height and no planting date. The park opened in 1926, but that is the park's date, not the tree's, and no source says the kapok went in with it. If you know when it was planted, or have measured it, tell us.

The park is free, on the edge of the city centre where the Rambla runs past it, about twelve minutes on foot from Plaza de la Candelaria.

trees.name: Old Tamarind of Parque García Sanabria

location.address: Parque Garcia Sanabria, Santa Cruz de Tenerife

trees.story:
The botanist who co-wrote Santa Cruz's catalogue of singular trees called an old tamarind the most veteran tree in the whole of Parque García Sanabria. Wolfredo Wildpret said so on a walk through the park with Diario de Avisos in 2018, and he remembered something better than a measurement. Its pods used to be sold as sweets from a cart at the side of the park, the cart people called the grandfather's.

There is one honest gap. The city register lists exactly one tamarind in the park, and this is it, but no source ties that register entry to the tree Wildpret pointed at in so many words. It is very probably the same tree. Probably is the right word.

Nobody has dated it either. The park opened in 1926, and Wildpret suggested that a carob nearby may be older than the park itself, from the years when the land was still farmed. He made no such claim for the tamarind. Spanish Wikipedia counts it among the biggest and oldest trees in the city, which is as far as the record goes. If you know its age, tell us.

Tamarind is a tropical tree grown for those brown, sticky, sweet-sour pods, which still end up in sweets around the world.

The park is free, at the edge of the city centre, about twelve minutes on foot from Plaza de la Candelaria.

trees.name: Banyan of Parque García Sanabria

location.address: Parque Garcia Sanabria, Santa Cruz de Tenerife

trees.story:
Parque García Sanabria's figs were a gift. According to Spanish Wikipedia, the park's collection of Ficus came from the Jardín de Aclimatación de La Orotava, the eighteenth-century garden at Puerto de la Cruz that also grows El Gran Ficus, and that collection includes some of the biggest and oldest trees in the city. Whether this banyan arrived with the gift, no source says.

It is on the city's register of singular trees as Ficus benghalensis, the banyan of India, a fig famous for dropping roots from its branches that thicken into pillars until one tree reads as a grove. That register entry is, for now, the whole of its paperwork. No second source names this tree, gives its girth or says when it was planted, and in a park with several kinds of fig a second opinion on the species would be welcome. If you know your figs, or know the tree, tell us.

Do not mistake it for its neighbours. The park also keeps Moreton Bay figs with hanging roots beside the bamboo path, and they look the part just as well. The park opened in 1926, but the banyan's own start date is unknown, and the park's opening is no substitute for it.

It stands about 100 metres north of the park's old tamarind and a little west of the great kapok, so the three make a short loop. The park is free, about twelve minutes on foot from Plaza de la Candelaria.

trees.name: Dragon Tree of Plaza del Chicharro

location.address: Plaza del Chicharro, Santa Cruz de Tenerife

trees.story:
Santa Cruz lists only seven dragon trees in its catalogue of singular trees, and this one shares a small square with a monument to a fish. Plaza del Chicharro is named for the chicharro, and the fish sculpture stands right beside the tree, close enough that it can hide the trunk from the wrong side of the square.

The tree is on the city's register and on the municipal route of singular trees, and that is most of what is written about it. There is no recorded height, no girth and no planting date. With this species the gap has a reason beyond missing paperwork. A dragon tree lays down no annual rings, so nobody can count years in its trunk. The island's Cabildo estimates the age of its listed dragon trees by counting the levels at which the crown has forked instead, and nobody has published that count for this one. If you have counted, or know when it was planted, tell us.

Dracaena draco is a native of the Canary Islands, and the island's monumental dragons stand in Icod de los Vinos, Tacoronte and La Orotava. This is the city's quieter version, a few minutes from the laurel figs of Plaza del Príncipe and the Moreton Bay figs of Plaza de San Francisco, which makes it an easy stop between the two.

The square is free and open, about four minutes on foot from Plaza de la Candelaria.

trees.name: Dragon Tree by the Iglesia de la Concepción

location.address: Calle Santo Domingo, Iglesia de Nuestra Senora de la Concepcion, Santa Cruz de Tenerife

location_site.name: Plaza de la Iglesia / Iglesia de la Concepcion

trees.story:
A dragon tree from the Canaries' own flora stands at the foot of a church bell tower in the island's capital. The fourth route of the municipal walk, as Tenerife Weekly described it in 2022, runs between the Teatro Guimerá and the church and names four things around the square. There is this dragon tree, an Australian pine, a crested Euphorbia and a pair of Indian laurel figs.

It is one of seven dragon trees the city catalogue lists. Beyond its place on the register and the route, nobody has published a height, a girth or a planting date. That is not unusual for the species. A dragon tree lays down no annual rings, so its years cannot be counted in the trunk, and the island's Cabildo estimates the age of its listed dragons by counting how many times the crown has forked. For this one, nobody has counted in print. If you know its age, or when it was planted, tell us.

The square repays a few minutes beyond the dragon. The two Indian laurel figs share it, and the council says most of the city's laurels are past their hundredth year, though nobody has dated these two in particular.

The church surroundings are free and open, about five minutes on foot from Plaza de la Candelaria, and about 400 metres from the Moreton Bay figs of Plaza de San Francisco.

trees.name: River Red Gum of Parque de La Granja

location.address: Parque de La Granja, Santa Cruz de Tenerife

trees.story:
An Australian gum tree shares the title of tallest tree in urban Santa Cruz with a pair of figs planted in 1864. The municipal catalogue of singular trees, as Diario de Avisos reported it in 2018, names this river red gum in Parque de La Granja alongside the laurel figs of Plaza del Príncipe as the tallest in the urban area. The figs are given 20 metres. The gum's own height is not given, which leaves the comparison to your eye.

Its girth is a small puzzle. The same report records 9.2 metres at the base and 10.25 metres in the trunk, which is the wrong way round for most trees, so one of the two figures is probably a slip in transcription. Either way it has one of the largest girths in the municipality.

The trunk is pale and divides into several stems, and it stands in a stone ring with a sign beside it. The route of singular trees through La Granja pairs it with an ombú from South America and a gum arabic tree. Nobody has published when it was planted or how old it is; if you know, tell us. The most recent dated sighting we can point to is from 2023, and a report from anyone who has stood under it since is welcome.

The park is free, about fifteen minutes on foot west of Plaza de la Candelaria, and city buses serve the area.

Sanity: a 9-10 m girth red gum is large but plausible. The park was closed for works in some years; access not rechecked. Flag: one press figure with internal inconsistency, alive evidence 2023.

trees.name: Ombú of Parque de La Granja

location.address: Parque de La Granja, Santa Cruz de Tenerife

trees.story:
The ombú looks like the oldest thing in any park it stands in, and botanically it is barely a tree. Phytolacca dioica is a giant herb from the South American pampas, with soft, water-filled wood rather than timber, and a base that swells and spreads with age until the trunk seems to melt into the ground. It grows fast, which is why a big one can look far older than it is.

This one is on the route of singular trees through Parque de La Granja. A 2022 description of the walk, from the Cepsa Foundation that backed it, runs from the ombú of South America to a gum arabic tree and the Australian red gum that shares the title of tallest tree in urban Santa Cruz. The city's register lists the ombú among its singular trees, and an iNaturalist observer recorded it, a few metres from the register's pin, in October 2025.

That is the extent of the written record. Nobody has published a girth, a height or a planting date for it, and for a species this deceptive no guess from its looks would be worth printing. If you know when it went in, tell us.

The red gum stands about 140 metres away, so the two make a single stop. The park is free, about fifteen minutes on foot west of Plaza de la Candelaria, at the far western end of a walk past the old trees of the centre.
